findings.body:
Removing the `ALLOWED_HOSTS` check lets `deliver()` POST to any caller-supplied URL. If customers can set `url`, this is classic SSRF: the server will hit internal hosts (e.g. `http://169.254.169.254/`, `http://localhost:…`, RFC1918) and `urlopen` will follow redirects.

Restore host validation before the request. For customer endpoints, allow only `https` and public hostnames (deny localhost, link-local, private ranges, and metadata IPs), or route through a locked-down egress proxy — do not call `urlopen` on a raw customer URL with no checks.

summary:
## Verdict

**Do not merge** — this change removes the only host allowlist on outbound webhook delivery and turns `deliver()` into an open server-side request proxy.

## Analysis

`webhooks.py` previously rejected any URL whose hostname was outside `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (`hooks.internal.example`). The PR deletes that check and posts directly to the caller-supplied `url` via `urllib.request.urlopen`.

Any caller that can influence `url` (customer webhook config, API input, stored endpoint) can force the runner/service to POST attacker-chosen destinations, including link-local metadata (`169.254.169.254`), localhost admin ports, and internal RFC1918 hosts. `urlopen` also follows redirects by default, which widens the blast radius after the first hop.

Supporting customer-owned endpoints is a valid product goal; it needs an allowlist/denylist (block private/link-local/metadata ranges), scheme restriction (`https` only), and preferably a pinned egress proxy — not an unconditional fetch.

**Recommendation:** request-changes

verification.reason: The patch removes the ALLOWED_HOSTS check that previously rejected non-allowlisted hosts; deliver() now POSTs via urlopen to any caller-supplied URL, and the new comment states endpoints are customer-provided—classic SSRF with no remaining guard.
